title: Not from desire
hook: by the star, your companion is not astray, nor does he speak from desire (53:1–3)
carry: you know better the affairs of your world
tomorrow: The lote tree of the boundary

segments.voice: Yesterday, tasbih, and your line was as the stars fade. Were you awake for the last stars, or close to it? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

A young man named 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr used to write down everything the Prophet ﷺ said. Every word. Some men of Quraysh told him to stop: he's a human being, they said, he speaks in anger and in good moods; why write it all? So 'Abdullah stopped, and went to ask. The Prophet pointed to his own mouth and told him to keep writing. Nothing comes out of this, he said, except truth. Today's surah has a verse behind that answer.

Surah An-Najm, the Star, the fifty-third, opens with one oath. Pickthall's translation: "By the Star when it setteth, Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived; Nor doth he speak of (his own) desire." Which star? Commentators differ. Some say the Pleiades; some say a falling star; some say any star at its setting. The oath is by something going down, out of sight, while what the surah defends stays. Then: your comrade, sahibukum. Not the Prophet or the Messenger, but your companion, the man who grew up among you. The verse speaks to people who knew him. Then the key line: wa ma yantiqu 'anil-hawa. Nor does he speak from desire. You've met that word: hawa, the desire that pulls you along, from the day we read desire as a god. Here the surah says the one bringing the message isn't driven by it. The next verse says: it is nothing but revelation revealed. How far does that reach? Scholars have discussed it carefully. It covers the Qur'an, first of all. Sunni scholarship has long held that his teaching in religious matters, the Sunnah, also rests on revelation in a broader sense, one reason hadith became a source of law. And scholars also point to a report where he gave an opinion in a worldly matter, how to pollinate date palms, and later said: you know better the affairs of your world. On this reading, the verse isn't a claim that he never had a personal view. It's a claim about the message: it isn't self-serving, and it isn't his wanting dressed up as revelation.
screen: `BY THE STAR AS IT SETS.` · `SAHIBUKUM: THE COMPANION YOU KNOW.` · `NOT FROM HAWA, BUT REVELATION.` · `HOW FAR IT REACHES: SCHOLARS WEIGH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak without self-interest once. Sit, and breathe. Think of a conversation coming up today: advice you'll give, a recommendation, a review, an opinion at work. Ask yourself honestly where your words might lean toward what you want: looking good, winning, getting your way. Choose one place to say what's true and useful for the other person, even if it gains you nothing. If you pray, you can ask for an honest tongue. The bell holds the time.
Hawa: the desire that pulls a person along; 53:3 says the Prophet does not speak from it, only revelation. Today's word.
Your line: you know better the affairs of your world. Today, before you give one piece of advice, check whether it serves them or you, and adjust it. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 53:3–4 as a basis for following the Prophet's Sunnah alongside the Qur'an, and scholars of hadith built careful methods for recording and checking his words.

original.note: Arabic: nor does he speak from desire (53:3).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Prophet never had a personal opinion.
what it means: the message he brought isn't his own wanting; it is revelation.
what a scholar hears: 53:3–4 is read first as the Qur'an, and in Sunni scholarship as the Sunnah too; the date-palm report (Sahih Muslim 2363) marks worldly opinion.
